piezas.titulo: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
piezas.resumenOriginal: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. piezas.titulo: Post-acute traumatic brain injury recovery: architecture of an illustrative curated evidence registry
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionTraumatic brain injury (TBI) recovery is shaped by secondary neuroinflammatory and neurovascular responses, injury severity, pre-injury health, rehabilitation timing and care setting. Yet rehabilitation evidence is commonly organized around interventions rather than the clinical decision context in which an intervention is considered.MethodsWe developed TBI-RECOVER to describe the architecture of a curated post-acute TBI recovery evidence registry across clinical decision-context signals, recovery domains, outcomes, care settings and nominal source roles. English-language PubMed records from database inception to 21 August 2026 were retrieved through seven complementary recovery-oriented search strands. Exact queries, PMIDs, XML metadata, retrieval failures and rule-based triage decisions were archived. An illustrative 50-source curated registry of guidelines, consensus documents and high-level evidence syntheses was assembled from returned records. Each entry received a primary recovery domain, a nominal source-role category, severity, recovery-time, care-setting, age and comorbidity reporting signals, and one or more outcome labels. Selection rationales were recorded for every entry; no numerical domain quota was used.ResultsThe curated registry comprised 50 sources after title/abstract and multidisciplinary re-audit: 10 guidelines or consensus documents, 16 intervention syntheses, 10 implementation or service-evidence sources, 13 measurement or prognostic-evidence sources and one protocol or methods source. Forty-six entries occupied the score 12 or higher triage stratum. Independent stratified manual relevance validation confirmed the original triage assignments, and multidisciplinary review confirmed the prespecified source-role and primary-domain classifications. The stored score was reproduced exactly for all 2,529 parsed records. Age language was absent in 23 sources, and no molecular/biochemical marker, cell-type or brain-region signal was present in the curated title/abstract metadata.DiscussionTBI-RECOVER provides a transparent structure for locating high-level recovery evidence, specifying clinical decision-context fields for future synthesis, and designing stratified rehabilitation and implementation studies.

piezas.titulo: An exploratory study of relationships between the executive functions and spatiotemporal control in a complex motor task: the spatial tapping task
piezas.resumenOriginal: Executive functions (EFs) are cognitive processes enabling planning, control, and regulation of behavior. A variety of tasks have been developed to evaluate EFs, from complex reasoning to simpler inhibition tasks, reflecting the diversity of symptoms observed in patients with executive deficits. Recent research has emphasized their unity, proposing three core functions, working memory, inhibition, and switching, that share resources and combine to enable complex tasks. Yet, no single task captures both the unity and diversity of EFs, limiting the development of a unified framework and a balanced assessment. To address this gap, we designed the spatial tapping task, a timing paradigm combining finger tapping and circle drawing. Finger tapping requires working memory for explicit timing control, whereas circle drawing requires anticipatory control akin to switching to control movement trajectory, enabling implicit timing control. Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. A slow tempo favors discrete movements with long pauses between taps, whereas a fast tempo promotes continuous motion. Previous analyses supported a change in timing control mode with increasing tempo. Here, we explored the hypothesis that EFs are engaged accordingly: working memory in the slow/discrete phase, switching in the fast/continuous phase, and inhibition in the intermediate phase, where demands for continuous motion increase. In two studies combined into a single dataset, we compared scores with those from neuropsychological tests using correlations. We found that timing accuracy in the slow/discrete phase was associated with working memory, spatial accuracy in the fast/continuous phase with switching, and longer contact time in the intermediate phase with inhibition. We also explored whether performance was consistent with the EF deficits described in the literature, and the potential contribution of motor output, reporting scores obtained across populations with executive deficits (aging and dementia), combined executive and motor impairments (schizophrenia), and motor expertise (biscriptual writers), along with matched controls. Findings were consistent, although often more specific, and highlighted an important contribution of motor output. Altogether, our results provide initial evidence that the task can be used to investigate EFs, although cognitive, motor, and sensory contributions need to be disentangled to improve its specificity.

piezas.titulo: Spatial working memory enhances gamma oscillations in rodent olfactory bulb and medial prefrontal cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: Spatial working memory (SWM), a specialized form of working memory that temporarily encodes and retains spatial information, is fundamental to guide animal behaviors, yet our current knowledge of its circuit mechanisms remains far from known. Since, olfactory bulb (OB) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are critical brain structures for a wide range of cognitive behaviors, we hypothesized that the OB-mPFC circuit gamma oscillations might support rodent SWM processing. Our results show that SWM enhances regional low (30-60 Hz), but not high (60-100 Hz), gamma oscillations in both OB and mPFC, in correlation with the animals behavioral performance. Additionally, the OB-mPFC gamma band functional connectivity is strengthened by SWM. Moreover, we find that mPFC gamma oscillatory information transfer to OB supports the animals SWM performance. We also show that OB low gamma oscillations are modulated by mPFC delta phase, which further signifies the roles of mPFC feedbacks to shape OB gamma activity during SWM. These results suggest that OB-mPFC circuit gamma rhythms underlie SWM processing, and point towards possible mechanisms for cognitive disorders.
